paras: The suspected lynching of Cleveland Kelly was the disappearance of Kelly, a 19-year-old Black man, in July 1903 while a posse pursued him into a swamp near Newborn, Newton County, Georgia. The posse returned saying it had lost him, but a dispatch from Madison, Georgia, reprinted widely in the white press, said it was "almost absolutely certain" that he had been captured and lynched. No report of a body, an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage, and the killing was never confirmed beyond that belief and a later news digest's statement that he "was lynched near Madison, Ga."

According to the Savannah Morning News of July 12, Kelly was accused of having attempted, on Wednesday, July 8, to assault Mrs. Will Robertson at Newborn while her husband was away. The paper said Will Robertson, working in a nearby field, heard his wife's cries, reached her in time, and fired at Kelly several times but missed. By then two posses were reported to be in pursuit.

A special to the Atlanta Constitution from Madison, dated July 13, reported that Kelly had disappeared. He was last heard from heading toward a swamp with "a posse of determined men close on his trail." The men came back a few hours later and said they had lost Kelly in the swamp and abandoned all efforts to capture him. The correspondent did not accept their account, writing that it was "almost absolutely certain, however, that the negro was captured and lynched."

No report of a body being found, an inquest, arrests or a later sighting of Kelly appears in the coverage. On July 24 the Newark Journal's "News of the World" column stated, without further detail, that Kelley, "a negro charged with assaulting a white woman," had been lynched near Madison.

The Madison dispatch appeared on July 14 in Southern papers including the Montgomery Advertiser, the Savannah Morning News and the Birmingham Age-Herald. Over the next week it ran, often abridged, as far away as Louisville, Raleigh, Abilene, Kansas, and Westminster, Maryland. Every version repeated the accusation as fact, describing Kelly as "the negro who attempted a criminal assault" on Mrs. Robertson.

Headlines differed in how far they credited the posse's story. Some treated the lynching as likely or settled, among them the Montgomery Advertiser's "Belief Prevails That He Was Lynched By Mob" and the Daily Morning Journal and Courier's "Undoubtedly Lynched." Others put the posse's claim in quotation marks or called it into question, as in the Savannah Morning News's "They 'Lost' the Negro," the Lancaster Ledger's "Merely 'Lost,'" and the Birmingham Age-Herald's "Posse Returns and Tells a Doubtful Story of Chase." Several shortened versions dropped the sentence about lynching altogether; the Omaha Daily Bee still headed its item "Swamp Gobbles Negro Up" and called the posse a "Lynching Party," while the Bemidji Daily Pioneer used "Negro Eludes Posse."
No report of the case was found in the Black press, so every known account comes from white papers relaying the single Madison dispatch.

Accounts of Kelly's fate diverged within the same dispatch: the posse said it had lost him in the swamp, while the correspondent believed he had been caught and lynched, giving no further basis for that belief. The Newark Journal's later statement that he was lynched added no names, date or details.

reader.title: Suspected lynching of Cleveland Kelly
bases: Kelly, accused of an attempted assault, was hunted by posses and disappeared in a swamp; the Madison dispatch said he was almost certainly captured and lynched (A1, A2) and a later digest said he was lynched (A16).

No body, killing or perpetrator is reported; the only evidence of death is the Madison correspondent's belief that the posse captured and lynched Kelly (A2) and a later digest's unsupported statement (A16), against the posse's own claim that it lost him (A2). If he was killed, it was by a pursuing posse of 'determined men' acting on an assault accusation without legal process (A1, A2).

Two posses and the accusation are reported in one Savannah item (A1); every report of the disappearance and suspected lynching traces to a single Constitution special from Madison (A2, A4, A5), and the later digest (A16) adds nothing independent.
